summary: "Putting a single mirror on a robot's tabletop drops manipulation success by 10.8 to 56.7 points across five policies - and 50 to 88 percent of the failures happen without the robot ever touching the mirror, pointing at phantom targeting and spatial mislocalization rather than collision."

Most robot benchmarks deliberately remove every nuisance from the scene. A new one puts a mirror back in. **RoboDojo-Mirror** (Xuanchen Liu and colleagues, iPPLab) extends RoboDojo while preserving task objectives, success criteria and policy checkpoints, so the *only* variable is reflection: a mirror-free baseline against **single-mirror**, **dual-mirror** and **mirrored-tabletop** conditions.

Every mirror condition degrades every policy. Averaged across the three mirror setups, the aggregate success drop ranges from **10.8 to 56.7 percentage points** depending on the policy, and reaches **62.5 points** on the mirrored tabletop. Five policies were tested, spanning **Vision-Language-Action models, World Action Models and agentic policies** - three distinct families of control stack, one shared weakness.

The obvious explanation is that a mirror is also a physical obstacle. The authors test that directly by comparing against geometrically matched **non-reflective panels**. The result rules it out: **50 to 88 percent** of mirror-specific failures occur **without any recorded robot-panel contact**. Collisions do not explain the degradation.

What the trajectory and contact analysis shows instead is **phantom targeting** of reflected objects and **spatial mislocalization** of real ones. The policies are not bumping into the mirror; they are reaching for the wrong thing, or reaching for the right thing in the wrong place. Targeted diagnostics add the detail: grasping near reflections degrades, pushing progress becomes policy-dependent, and physical-target interaction collapses when the main camera's view is occluded. Real-robot experiments with **π0.5** and **FastWAM** reproduce the pattern - lower success rates under the upright-mirror and mirrored-tabletop conditions, so this is not a simulator artifact.

The broader implication is bigger than mirrors. Every deployment environment with reflective surfaces - a stainless steel counter, a glossy black tabletop, a window, a display - hands these policies a phantom object and a corrupted spatial frame. And the failure mode is silent: the robot does not crash, it just reaches for something that is not there, or reaches in the wrong direction, with no signal that anything went wrong.

Practical read: reflective surfaces belong in your evaluation suite even if they never appear in your training data. If you are deploying embodied policies in homes, labs or kitchens, a single mirror panel is a cheap, brutal diagnostic for whether the policy is reading the scene or reading its own assumptions about the scene.

Source: [arXiv:2611.33010 - Embodied AI Fails the Mirror Test: How a Simple Mirror Breaks Robot Policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.33010)
